title: Bunuelos Colombianos
subtitle: Fried cheese fritters traditional at Christmas
excerpt: Light, hollow cheese fritters made from tapioca flour and fresh white cheese, fried until golden and puffed. This recipe makes 20 bunuelos and takes about 35 minutes. In Colombia these are the taste of Christmas, eaten warm from the pan with a mug of hot chocolate.
sourceNotes: Bunuelos are eaten throughout Latin America but the Colombian version made with fresh white cheese and cassava starch is particularly associated with Christmas celebrations. Families make large batches during December and they are sold by street vendors at festive markets. The light, hollow fritters are often eaten with natilla (a corn custard).

recipe.batchNotes: Make large batches for gatherings. The dough holds in the fridge for up to 2 hours before frying.

content.text: This recipe makes 20 bunuelos and takes about 35 minutes. The dough is simple to mix and requires no resting time. The key to the characteristic hollow centre is frying at the right temperature: the dough puffs in the hot oil, the outside sets, and the inside steams into a light, airy pocket.

Use queso blanco, queso fresco or any mild white cheese that is not too salty and grates or crumbles easily. Mature cheddar is too sharp and will overpower the delicate flavour. The dough should feel soft and tacky but hold together; if it is too wet the bunuelos will not hold their shape in the oil. Fry in small batches so the oil temperature stays steady at around 170C: too hot and they brown before puffing, too cool and they absorb the oil.
Combine the tapioca flour, sugar, 1 tsp baking powder and a pinch of salt in a bowl. Add 200g finely grated or crumbled queso blanco or mild white cheese and mix to combine.
Beat the eggs and add to the flour and cheese mixture. Mix until it comes together into a dough. Add 2 tbsp whole milk if the dough is too dry to come together, adding it a tablespoon at a time.
Roll the dough into walnut-sized balls, about 20 in total. Keep them covered with a damp cloth while you heat the oil.
Heat vegetable oil to 170C in a deep, heavy pan. You need enough oil to submerge the bunuelos; at least 5cm deep.

Fry in batches of 4 to 5, turning occasionally, for 4 to 6 minutes until evenly golden and puffed. The bunuelos will float and should be turned to colour evenly. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.
Serve immediately while still warm. They deflate slightly as they cool and are best eaten within 10 minutes of frying.

attrs.symptom: Bunuelos are not puffing up in the oil
attrs.cause: Oil temperature is too low, or the baking powder is old and not active
attrs.fix: Check the oil is at 170C before adding the bunuelos. Test with a small piece of dough first: it should rise to the surface within 5 seconds. Replace the baking powder if it is over 6 months old.

attrs.symptom: Bunuelos are browning on the outside but doughy inside
attrs.cause: Oil is too hot and the outside is cooking before the inside has time to steam and cook through
attrs.fix: Reduce the oil temperature to 165C to 170C. Use a thermometer rather than guessing. Smaller balls will cook through more evenly.

attrs.symptom: Dough is too wet to roll into balls
attrs.cause: Too much milk added, or the cheese was very wet
attrs.fix: Add extra tapioca flour a tablespoon at a time until the dough holds its shape. Pat wet cheese dry with kitchen paper before grating or crumbling into the dough.

content.text: From December onwards, the smell of bunuelos frying is everywhere in Colombia: in family kitchens, at street markets and in the entrances of shops. They are paired with natilla, a thick corn custard, and eaten warm on Christmas Eve. Outside Colombia they are found wherever Colombian communities celebrate the festive season. If you have never eaten one fresh from the oil, it is hard to explain how light they are for something fried.
